book.title: Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction
book.author: Philip E. Tetlock, Dan Gardner

chapters.title: An Optimistic Skeptic
chapters.hook: The famous voice sounds certain, but the quiet clerk with a score sheet keeps getting closer.
chapters.counterintuition: Branka assumes the best forecaster will sound confident and senior. The useful signal is a checked record, not status, and the right stance is effort with limits in view.
chapters.tryThisNow: Open a note, write one forecast you already believe about a public forecast, add a percent and a check date, then write what would make you move the number down.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Trust forecasts by the record they expose, not by the confidence they perform; respect real uncertainty, then work the questions where feedback can still improve judgment.

Write the odds where the room can see them. Add the date, the question, and the sign that would make you change your mind. The record is the part of confidence that survives the room.

A forecast gets useful when it can be checked later. Confidence without a receipt is only weather in someone else's voice. Keep the receipt.

At 9:05 p.m., Branka, a city-budget aide, sits under a buzzing light with two growth forecasts open. The confident memo has a mayor’s signature. The ugly spreadsheet has last year’s errors marked in red. The easy move is to pick the story that feels whole. The better move is to slow down long enough to ask what the record says before this case arrived.

A number is not a costume for certainty. It is a handle. You can move it when the facts move. You can also leave it alone when the new fact is only loud. A number is not a costume for certainty. It is a handle.

Picture Rakel at a school-board table, asked to choose between a famous consultant and a dull local forecast with five years of scores. The choice is not between swagger and silence. The choice is between a claim that can learn and a claim that can only defend itself.

breakdown.fullRead:
At 4:18 p.m., Haldor, a port dispatcher, watches fog thicken over the harbor cameras. A veteran captain says the delay will clear by dusk, but the logbook on Haldor’s desk says fog like this has held past midnight four times this month. Everyone at the table can feel the pull of a clean story. It lowers stress. It gives the next meeting a script. It also hides the weak joint in the forecast, the part nobody will remember to test unless someone writes it down now.

Hand the room a sharper question. Do not ask whether the whole future will go well. Ask whether a named event will happen by a named date. Ask what would count as yes. Ask what rate similar cases have shown before. The room may groan, because the work feels smaller. The smaller work is the point. It gives reality a place to answer.

A forecaster earns trust by leaving tracks. The first track is the base rate. Before you explain why this case is special, look at how often cases like it have turned out that way. The second track is the update. If a new fact arrives, move the odds by the strength of that fact, not by the size of the feeling it creates. The third track is the review. When the result lands, save the old number and ask which assumption broke.

At 11:30 a.m., Valdis, a grants officer, reads a disaster-prep proposal with a glossy cover. She writes 35 percent in the margin, then adds a note about what would move her to 50. This is where the craft starts to feel almost physical. The pen pauses. The number changes from 60 to 55, not from 60 to 10, because the new fact is real but not huge. The team can see the move. Nobody has to pretend the old answer was perfect.

A forecast with tracks can be corrected; a forecast with only tone can only be admired. It keeps judgment from turning into a costume. A person can sound brave while hiding from the record. A quieter person with dates, odds, and reviews may be doing the harder thing.

The limit matters. Long-range shocks, hidden incentives, and fragile systems can make even careful work miss. A good forecaster does not use that as an excuse to blur every claim. She uses it to sort questions. Some deserve a wide range. Some deserve a backup plan. Some deserve no forecast stronger than a shrug.

Try the move on a live claim today. Take one future sentence you hear at work, at home, or in the news. Cut it into a smaller question. Put a probability on it. Write why you chose that number. Then mark the date when you will look again. The act takes two minutes. The habit changes the room because it makes confidence answerable.

examples.title: Branka puts a score sheet under the keynote flyer

planSpec.audience: a deputy budget director choosing which revenue forecast to brief
planSpec.stakes: whether a hiring freeze is triggered by reputation or record
planSpec.requiredBeat: she checks the speaker’s past calls before trusting his new one

examples.scenario: Branka clips a blue pen to the city hall clipboard at 7:12 a.m. in the finance office, with the keynote speaker's glossy flyer under her thumb. The mayor wants his revenue forecast in the noon packet. Beside the flyer is a dull spreadsheet from a retired clerk who has tracked every local sales-tax call since 2018. Branka is about to paste the famous forecast into the packet, but the clerk's error column is open on her screen and she has to decide which record gets the first line.
examples.whatToDo: Check the scored record before using the famous forecast. Put the clerk's past hits and misses beside the speaker's claims, then brief the number with the better trail.
examples.whyItMatters: Prestige can make a forecast feel safer than it is. A written record gives the team something firmer to trust and something to revisit when the quarter closes.

examples.title: Keiji weighs the radio voice against the rain gauge

planSpec.audience: a vineyard manager deciding whether to pick early
planSpec.stakes: whether a whole block of grapes gets pulled before the storm
planSpec.requiredBeat: he compares the confident radio forecast with his own logged microclimate data

examples.scenario: Keiji wipes dust from the brass rain gauge at 5:36 a.m. behind the north block of vines. The radio host says the storm will miss the valley, warm voice, no odds. Keiji's notebook says this hill catches rain whenever the coast buoy drops fast, and the buoy reading is blinking on his phone. The picking crew is waiting by the trucks. He is about to wave them home, but his thumb hovers over the group text and he has to decide which signal deserves the day.
examples.whatToDo: Use the local record first. Check the buoy pattern against prior storms, put a probability on rain by noon, and choose the harvest plan from that number, not from the radio voice.
examples.whyItMatters: The forecast is local work. A confident outside voice may be useful, but Keiji's logged hill data knows the exact slope the grapes are sitting on.

examples.title: Rakel circles the missed arrivals in orange

planSpec.audience: a route supervisor reviewing bad bus-delay predictions
planSpec.stakes: whether tomorrow’s schedule keeps hiding weak estimates
planSpec.requiredBeat: she preserves the wrong forecast instead of smoothing it after the buses arrive

examples.scenario: Rakel sits in the bus depot break room at 10:48 p.m., orange marker uncapped, last night's arrival board printed on legal paper. The dispatch forecast had said the Route 12 delays would clear by 6:00. The buses were still stacked at 7:20. Her first instinct is to edit the note before sending it upstairs, changing will clear to may clear. She stops with the marker tip touching the page. The wrong words are the only part that can teach tomorrow's shift.
examples.whatToDo: Leave the original wording alone. Circle the miss, write the actual arrival times beside it, and add one sentence about which assumption failed.
examples.whyItMatters: Learning needs the old claim intact. If the miss is softened after the outcome, the team protects pride and loses the reason the next estimate could improve.

examples.title: Haldor reads the fog log before clearing berth seven

planSpec.audience: a harbor dispatcher under pressure from a late container ship
planSpec.stakes: whether a risky docking call is based on veteran confidence or scored patterns
planSpec.requiredBeat: he predicts from the log, then watches the fog confirm the lower-confidence call

examples.scenario: Haldor sets the laminated fog log beside berth seven's radio at 4:18 p.m., while the container ship Kestrel asks for clearance. Captain Rusk says he has seen this burn off a hundred times. Haldor writes his own odds, 30 percent clear by dusk, because the last four north-wind fogs held past midnight. The pilot boat is idling. He has to decide whether to trust the captain's memory or the log before the clearance window closes. At 6:50, the camera still shows gray water.
examples.whatToDo: Make the call from the logged pattern and state the odds aloud. Delay clearance unless a fresh signal changes the number before the window closes.
examples.whyItMatters: The captain's memory may be rich, but it is not scored. The log turns past weather into a check on the story the room wants to believe.

examples.title: Valdis writes thirty-five percent in the grant margin

planSpec.audience: a grants officer rating a disaster-prep proposal
planSpec.stakes: whether a glossy proposal gets treated as reliable planning
planSpec.requiredBeat: she notices her confidence rising because of polish and writes a modest probability instead

examples.scenario: Valdis rests her hand on a glossy flood-prep proposal at 11:30 a.m. in the county grants office, the paper so thick it hardly bends. The photos are clean, the risk map is shaded, the executive summary feels finished. She can feel herself wanting to mark it strong. Then she sees the blank line for past delivery record. Her pen pauses over the score box. She writes 35 percent in the margin and sits with how plain the number looks.
examples.whatToDo: Name the uncertainty before scoring the proposal. Write the probability, list what record is missing, and ask for past delivery data before moving the number up.
examples.whyItMatters: Polish can create a feeling of proof. A modest number keeps the missing record visible, which protects the grant from being awarded to a mood.

examples.title: Nilo asks the seminar for last year’s odds

planSpec.audience: a residency teacher discussing a confident diagnosis prediction
planSpec.stakes: whether trainees learn to ask for records instead of credentials
planSpec.requiredBeat: he asks for the scored history behind a forecast during morning report

examples.scenario: Nilo taps chalk dust from his sleeve at 8:03 a.m. in the residency classroom. A visiting specialist has just predicted that the new triage rule will cut missed sepsis cases in half. The interns are nodding. Nilo points to the blank corner of the board. "What did this team predict last year, and what happened?" he asks. The room goes quiet. A senior resident reaches for her laptop. reviewCards.front: You hear a confident claim about a public forecast. What do you ask before trusting it?
reviewCards.back: Ask for the dated probability, the base rate, and the outcome that would count as a miss. Forecasts improve when they can be checked, not when they sound smooth.

reviewCards.front: A fresh story makes your estimate feel wrong. How should you update?
reviewCards.back: Move the odds by the strength of the new evidence. A vivid story can matter, but it should not erase the older record unless it directly changes the facts.

reviewCards.front: A team wants one bold answer. What smaller move protects learning?
reviewCards.back: Break the issue into dated subquestions. Smaller forecasts show which assumption failed, so the next estimate can improve instead of becoming a blame session.

reviewCards.front: A miss is embarrassing. What should the review preserve?
reviewCards.back: Keep the original wording and number. Then mark which assumption failed. The record has to sting a little or it will not teach.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is separating confidence from proof and keeping a written record that can correct you. Practice means writing the claim before the outcome arrives, then updating it in small, visible steps. The point is not to look cautious. The point is to give reality a way to train you.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a work meeting turns on a public forecast, then write one dated probability on the agenda and name the result that would prove it wrong.
If you are choosing a health step under uncertainty, then write the base rate you know, the personal fact that changes it, and the next check-in date.
If a personal plan depends on a guess, then split the guess into one small forecast you can check within seven days.
If someone you care about sounds certain about the future, then ask what evidence would make both of you lower the odds by ten points.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tomorrow night, write one live forecast about a public forecast with a date, a probability, and two reasons for the number. Put a reminder on the date to check it without rewriting the original line.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review one old forecast before you know the outcome. Move the number only if new evidence deserves it, and write the reason in one sentence.

examples.title: Vesta turns the cracked tablet toward the lab values

planSpec.audience: a nurse practitioner facing a tidy patient story
planSpec.stakes: whether a patient is sent home with the wrong cause named
planSpec.requiredBeat: she catches a story that feels complete before the labs fit

examples.scenario: Vesta steadies a cracked tablet at 8:22 a.m. in exam room three, the patient's cough history glowing in neat checkboxes. The story says simple bronchitis: no fever, no chest pain, no travel. Then the oxygen number blinks lower than it should and the pulse is climbing. Her hand is already moving toward the discharge instructions. She has to decide whether the clean story is knowledge or just the first story that stopped the search.
examples.whatToDo: Stop the discharge. Mark the story as a guess, not a finding, and list the two numbers that do not fit before choosing the next test.
examples.whyItMatters: A neat explanation can feel like closure before the case earns it. The mismatched numbers keep the search open long enough to protect the patient.

examples.title: Qadir waits for the hallway video to load

planSpec.audience: a counselor reviewing a parent’s confident account
planSpec.stakes: whether a student gets punished from a one-sided story
planSpec.requiredBeat: he separates the email’s claims from evidence before calling home

examples.scenario: Qadir holds a mug of mint tea at 3:47 p.m. in the middle-school counseling office while a parent email fills his screen. It explains the hallway fight perfectly: one child provoked, one child snapped, no mystery left. The video file is still loading in the corner, gray wheel spinning. The assistant principal wants a suspension call before buses leave. Qadir has to decide whether the smooth email counts as evidence or only as someone's map of it.
examples.whatToDo: Open a three-column note: seen, said, unknown. Put the email in said, wait for the video, and make no discipline call until the columns stop pretending to be the same.
examples.whyItMatters: The parent may be sincere and still incomplete. Sorting the source of each claim prevents the cleanest narrative from outrunning the facts.

examples.title: Linh reads the second server log after the outage memo

planSpec.audience: an incident lead reviewing a too-neat outage explanation
planSpec.stakes: whether the next outage review preserves real uncertainty
planSpec.requiredBeat: she finds the story blamed one server before the second log was checked

examples.scenario: Linh sits on the data-center floor at 11:16 p.m., knees against a cold cabinet door, rereading the outage memo on her phone. The draft says the payment crash came from Server A, clean and final. The second log, still open on her laptop, shows Server B timing out six minutes earlier. Her stomach drops. The neat story was written before the mess was read. She has to decide what rule tomorrow's review will carry.
examples.whatToDo: Rewrite the review around known, inferred, and unknown. Keep Server A as a factor, add Server B as unresolved, and assign the next check before closing the incident.
examples.whyItMatters: A postmortem that feels finished too soon trains the team to stop looking. Naming the unknown keeps the next outage from inheriting the same blind spot.

examples.title: Edric sees the proofing timer blinking behind the butter

planSpec.audience: a bakery owner diagnosing a failed batch before dawn
planSpec.stakes: whether he blames the wrong cause and repeats the error
planSpec.requiredBeat: he predicts butter failure, then the timer reveals a simpler miss

examples.scenario: Edric slides a tray of flat croissants onto the steel table at 7:05 a.m., steam carrying the sour smell of wasted butter. The apprentice says the new butter supplier is the problem, and Edric believes it for ten full seconds. He starts drafting the vendor text in his head. Then he sees the proofing timer behind the flour bin, still blinking from 3:40. He has to decide whether to keep the supplier story or admit the simpler cause in front of the crew.
examples.whatToDo: Check the physical record before blaming the supplier. Read the timer, compare it with the batch sheet, and say the error plainly while everyone can still see the evidence.
examples.whyItMatters: The supplier story protects pride because it points outside the room. The timer points to the process, which is the only part the bakery can fix today.

examples.title: Marna draws three boxes on the claims folder

planSpec.audience: a claims adjuster sorting a crash account
planSpec.stakes: whether fault is assigned from a vivid but incomplete account
planSpec.requiredBeat: she changes from one-story certainty to fact/guess/unknown columns

examples.scenario: At 2:18 p.m., Marna opens a red claims folder beside a dented bumper photo and almost writes driver at fault. The statement is vivid: wet road, sudden swerve, no time. Before, she would have trusted the detail. Today she draws three boxes on the folder: fact, guess, unknown. The missing traffic-camera video goes in unknown. The skid length goes in fact. By 4:00, the video shows a delivery van running the light. Her first story would have charged the wrong driver.
examples.whatToDo: Use three boxes before assigning fault. Put each item where it belongs and wait for the missing video or measurement before turning the story into a decision.
examples.whyItMatters: Vivid detail feels like accuracy, but it can still point at the wrong person. The boxes keep evidence from borrowing force from a confident narrator.

examples.title: Sol takes the crime-board photo down

planSpec.audience: a reporter revising a crime explanation under deadline
planSpec.stakes: whether a thin theory hardens into a published claim
planSpec.requiredBeat: he notices the photo wall making the theory feel more proven than it is

examples.scenario: Sol stands in the newsroom at 9:41 p.m., thumbtacks in his palm, looking at the photo wall he built around the burglary series. Red string links the same three faces. It looks convincing because he made it look convincing. The police scanner is quiet, the editor wants copy, and the only confirmed fact is the entry time. Sol pulls one photo down and feels the theory weaken. He has to decide whether to publish the tidy pattern or write what is still unknown.
examples.whatToDo: Print the story with the confirmed facts first and the theory clearly marked as a theory. Remove any visual cue that makes thin evidence look solved.
examples.whyItMatters: Presentation can create false confidence even for the person who built it. Naming uncertainty protects readers from inheriting the reporter's layout as proof.

chapters.title: What's Next?
chapters.hook: Forecasting gets better when institutions stop rewarding the blur and start checking the claim.
chapters.counterintuition: Icaro thinks better forecasts require better geniuses. The larger fix is cultural: clearer questions, visible scores, better incentives, and rewards for updating.
chapters.tryThisNow: Open a note, write one forecast you already believe about an institutional forecast, add a percent and a check date, then write what would make you move the number down.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Build forecasting cultures that ask clear questions, publish scores, reward updates, and make leaders prefer accountable uncertainty over confident blur.

breakdown.fastRead:
At 8:01 a.m., Icaro adds a score column to the agency forecast form. The form changes what people bother to write. He wants the clean answer now. The paper in front of him will not give it.

Write the odds where the room can see them. Add the date, the question, and the sign that would make you change your mind. A culture changes when the forecast has to come back and face its own receipt.

A forecast gets useful when it can be checked later. Confidence without a receipt is only weather in someone else's voice. Keep the receipt.
breakdown.deepRead:
At 3:16 p.m., Bethan, a foundation director, changes the grant review to ask for odds and later checks. Applicants stop hiding inside hopeful paragraphs. The easy move is to pick the story that feels whole. The better move is to slow down long enough to ask what the record says before this case arrived.

A number is not a costume for certainty. It is a handle. You can move it when the facts move. You can also leave it alone when the new fact is only loud. Clear questions are infrastructure for better judgment.

Picture Kumiko posting the product team’s old launch forecasts beside the new roadmap. The choice is not between swagger and silence. The choice is between a claim that can learn and a claim that can only defend itself.

Use the smallest clean question you can write. Put a date on it. Start from the outside view, the rate for cases like this one, then adjust for what is truly different here. Stop when you can explain the move in plain words.

A limit stays in view. Some events are too tangled, too far out, or too hidden for a sharp answer. The skill is not pretending fog is glass. The skill is knowing when the glass is only dirty enough to wipe.
breakdown.fullRead:
At 9:48 a.m., Rajiv, a school superintendent, asks vendors to show past forecast scores before selling software predictions. The room shifts when the pitch has to carry a record. Everyone at the table can feel the pull of a clean story. It lowers stress. It gives the next meeting a script. It also hides the weak joint in the forecast, the part nobody will remember to test unless someone writes it down now.

Hand the room a sharper question. Do not ask whether the whole future will go well. Ask whether a named event will happen by a named date. Ask what would count as yes. Ask what rate similar cases have shown before. The room may groan, because the work feels smaller. The smaller work is the point. It gives reality a place to answer.

A forecaster earns trust by leaving tracks. The first track is the base rate. Before you explain why this case is special, look at how often cases like it have turned out that way. The second track is the update. If a new fact arrives, move the odds by the strength of that fact, not by the size of the feeling it creates. The third track is the review. When the result lands, save the old number and ask which assumption broke.

At 5:27 p.m., Dorte, a city auditor, writes the first public forecast ledger for major projects. Nobody loves the ledger until it prevents the next soft promise. This is where the craft starts to feel almost physical. The pen pauses. The number changes from 60 to 55, not from 60 to 10, because the new fact is real but not huge. The team can see the move. Nobody has to pretend the old answer was perfect.

Reward the update, and people stop treating changed minds as damage. It keeps judgment from turning into a costume. A person can sound brave while hiding from the record. A quieter person with dates, odds, and reviews may be doing the harder thing.

The limit matters. Long-range shocks, hidden incentives, and fragile systems can make even careful work miss. A good forecaster does not use that as an excuse to blur every claim. She uses it to sort questions. Some deserve a wide range. Some deserve a backup plan. Some deserve no forecast stronger than a shrug.

Try the move on a live claim today. Take one future sentence you hear at work, at home, or in the news. Cut it into a smaller question. Put a probability on it. Write why you chose that number. Then mark the date when you will look again. The act takes two minutes. The habit changes the room because it makes confidence answerable.

examples.scenario: Before the quarterly roadmap, Kumiko's product teams remembered every slip as unavoidable. examples.title: Rajiv asks the vendor for past forecast scores

planSpec.audience: a superintendent buying predictive software
planSpec.stakes: whether a sales pitch must show a record

examples.scenario: Rajiv folds his hands at 9:48 a.m. in the district conference room while the software vendor shows a dropout-risk dashboard. The colors are elegant. "What were your last twenty district forecasts, and how were they scored?" he asks. The sales lead clicks back two slides, then stops. The school board members look up from the pastries. Rajiv has to decide whether to let the pitch continue without the record.
examples.whatToDo: Pause the pitch until the vendor shows scored forecasts from comparable districts. If no record exists, treat the claim as unproven.
examples.whyItMatters: A model that predicts students should carry a record before it shapes student lives. Pretty dashboards are not evidence of accuracy.

examples.title: Dorte writes the city’s first public project ledger

examples.scenario: Dorte sits in the council archive at 5:27 p.m., dust on her black cardigan, three project binders open around her. Each bridge repair forecast used different words: soon, likely, on track. Each overran. She opens a blank spreadsheet titled public forecast ledger and enters the next library renovation with date, odds, owner, and check point. Nobody asked for the ledger. The binders did.
examples.whatToDo: Create the public ledger and enter the next project before it starts. Track owner, probability, check date, and result.
examples.whyItMatters: Soft promises survive because they disappear into binders. A public ledger gives voters and managers the same memory.

examples.title: Yanis changes the bonus rule for updated forecasts

planSpec.audience: a strategy chief changing incentives
planSpec.stakes: whether people get rewarded for sounding certain or updating well

examples.scenario: Yanis edits the strategy-team bonus rubric at 7:04 p.m., city lights reflected in the window behind the spreadsheet. The old score rewarded bold calls that landed. examples.whatToDo: Reward evidence-based updates, not just bold initial calls. Score the final outcome and the quality of revisions along the way.
examples.whyItMatters: Incentives decide what people protect. If updates are punished, forecasters defend old numbers after the evidence has moved.

reviewCards.front: You hear a confident claim about an institutional forecast. What do you ask before trusting it?
reviewCards.back: Ask for the dated probability, the base rate, and the outcome that would count as a miss. Forecasts improve when they can be checked, not when they sound smooth.

reviewCards.front: A fresh story makes your estimate feel wrong. How should you update?
reviewCards.back: Move the odds by the strength of the new evidence. A vivid story can matter, but it should not erase the older record unless it directly changes the facts.

reviewCards.front: A team wants one bold answer. What smaller move protects learning?
reviewCards.back: Break the issue into dated subquestions. Smaller forecasts show which assumption failed, so the next estimate can improve instead of becoming a blame session.

reviewCards.front: A miss is embarrassing. What should the review preserve?
reviewCards.back: Keep the original wording and number. Then mark which assumption failed. The record has to sting a little or it will not teach.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is designing systems where forecasts are written, checked, updated, and rewarded for accuracy instead of confidence.
